[[File:Conformal map.svg|thumb|The upper manifold is flat. The lower one is not, but it is conformal to the first one]]
A ([[pseudo-Riemannian manifold|pseudo]]-)[[Riemannian manifold]] is '''conformally flat''' if each point has a neighborhood that can be mapped to [[Flat manifold|flat space]] by a [[conformal transformation]].

In practice, the [[metric tensor]] <math>g</math> of the manifold <math>M</math> has to be conformal to the flat metric tensor <math>\eta</math>, i.e., the [[Geodesic|geodesics]] maintain in all points of <math>M</math> the angles by moving from one to the other, as well as keeping the null geodesics unchanged,<ref name=":0">{{cite book |author=Ray D'Inverno |title=Introducing Einstein's Relativity |pages=88–89 |chapter=6.13 The Weyl tensor }}</ref> that means there exists a function <math>\lambda(x)</math> such that <math>g(x) = \lambda^2(x)\, \eta</math>, where <math>\lambda(x)</math> is known as the [[Conformal_geometry#Conformal_manifolds|conformal factor]] and <math>x</math> is a point on the manifold.

More formally, let <math>(M,g)</math> be a pseudo-Riemannian manifold. Then <math>(M,g)</math> is conformally flat if for each point <math>x</math> in <math>M</math>, there exists a neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>x</math> and a [[smooth function]] <math>f</math> defined on <math>U</math> such that <math>(U,e^{2f} g)</math> is [[flat manifold|flat]] (i.e. the [[Riemann curvature tensor|curvature]] of <math>e^{2f} g</math> vanishes on <math>U</math>). The function <math>f</math> need not be defined on all of <math>M</math>.

Some authors use the definition of '''locally conformally flat''' when referred to just some point <math>x</math> on <math>M</math> and reserve the definition of ''conformally flat'' for the case in which the relation is valid for all <math>x</math> on <math>M</math>.

== Examples ==
* Every manifold with [[constant curvature|constant]] [[sectional curvature]] is conformally flat.
* Every 2-dimensional pseudo-Riemannian manifold is conformally flat.<ref name=":0" />
** The [[line element]] of the two dimensional spherical coordinates, like the one used in the [[geographic coordinate system]], <math>ds^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2 \theta \, d\phi^2 </math>,<ref>See ''{{slink|Spherical coordinate system#Integration and differentiation in spherical coordinates}}''</ref> has metric tensor <math>\textstyle g_{ik} = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sin^2 \theta \end{smallmatrix} \right]</math> and is not flat but with the [[stereographic projection]] can be mapped to a flat space using the conformal factor <math>\textstyle \frac{2}{1+r^2}</math>, where <math>r</math> is the distance from the origin of the flat space,<ref>See ''{{slink|Stereographic projection#Properties}}'' – Riemann's formula</ref> obtaining <math>\textstyle ds^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2 \theta \, d\phi^2 \, = \frac{4}{(1+r^2)^2}(dx^2 +dy^2) </math>.
* A 3-dimensional pseudo-Riemannian manifold is conformally flat if and only if the [[Cotton tensor]] vanishes.
* An ''n''-dimensional pseudo-Riemannian manifold for ''n'' ≥ 4 is conformally flat if and only if the [[Weyl tensor]] vanishes.
* Every [[compact space|compact]], [[simply connected]], conformally Euclidean Riemannian manifold is conformally equivalent to the [[n-sphere|round sphere]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kuiper|first1=N. H.|title=On conformally flat spaces in the large|journal=Annals of Mathematics|date=1949|volume=50|issue=4|pages=916–924|doi=10.2307/1969587|jstor=1969587|ref=Kuiper}}</ref>
:* The [[stereographic projection]] provides a coordinate system for the sphere in which conformal flatness is explicit, as the metric is proportional to the flat one.
* In [[general relativity]], conformally flat manifolds are often used, for instance, in describing the [[Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Garecki |first=Janusz |year=2008 |title=On Energy of the Friedman Universes in Conformally Flat Coordinates |journal=Acta Physica Polonica B |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=781–797 |arxiv=0708.2783 |bibcode=2008AcPPB..39..781G}}</ref> However, this is not always possible, as in the case of the [[Kerr metric]], which does not admit any conformally flat slices.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Garat |first1=Alcides |last2=Price |first2=Richard H. |date=2000-05-18 |title=Nonexistence of conformally flat slices of the Kerr spacetime |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=61 |issue=12 |article-number=124011 |arxiv=gr-qc/0002013 |bibcode=2000PhRvD..61l4011G |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.61.124011 |issn=0556-2821 |s2cid=119452751}}</ref>{{explain|reason=What would be of interest here is whether a Kerr spacetime is conformally flat.  This is presumably implied by nonexistence of conformally flat slicing, but the article should make this clear.|date=July 2025}}
: An example of conformally flat metric can be obtained by transforming the [[Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates]] for the [[Schwarzschild metric]], which have line element <math>\textstyle ds^2 = \left(1-{2GM}/{r} \right) dv \, du</math>  with metric tensor <math>\textstyle g_{ik} = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1-{2GM}/{r} \\ 1-{2GM}/{r} & 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right] </math> and so is not flat. But with the transformations <math>t = (v + u)/2</math> and <math>x = (v - u)/2</math> becomes <math>\textstyle ds^2 = \left(1-{2GM}/{r} \right) (dt^2 - dx^2)</math> with metric tensor <math>\textstyle g_{ik} = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1-{2GM}/{r} & 0 \\ 0 & -1+{2GM}/{r} \end{smallmatrix} \right]</math>, which is the flat metric times the conformal factor <math>\textstyle 1-{2GM}/{r}</math>.<ref>{{cite book |author=Ray D'Inverno |title=Introducing Einstein's Relativity |pages=230–231 |chapter=17.2 The Kruskal solution }}</ref>
